profiles.name: Nancy H. Smith
profiles.description:
Nancy H. Smith — SOA Watch line-crosser at Fort Benning, Georgia. Convicted of trespass on a military installation and sentenced to 30 days in federal custody.

Each November on the anniversary of the assassination of six Jesuits, their housekeeper, and her daughter at the University of Central America in San Salvador in 1989, peace activists gather at the gates of Fort Benning, Georgia, site of the U.S. Army School of the Americas / Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC), to commemorate the dead and to call for the school's closure. Hundreds have crossed the line onto the base over four decades of vigils; many have served federal sentences ranging from 30 days to a year for trespass.
profiles.finding: SOA Watch roster supports identity; initial portrait search produced no verified individual image.

profiles.name: Vinh Tan Nguyen
profiles.description: Vinh Tan Nguyen, a Vietnamese-American age 63, was convicted of misuse of a passport to facilitate an act of international terrorism for his role in a plot to bomb the Vietnam Embassy in the Philippines. He admitted storing explosives and testing bombs in Manila. Sentenced to 14 months federal prison plus 2 years supervised release.
profiles.finding: Initial full-name embassy bombing search produced no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Suzanne Swift
profiles.description: Suzanne Swift was a U.S. Army military police specialist who served in Iraq and refused redeployment in January 2006 after reporting sexual harassment and abuse by fellow service members. On December 13, 2006, she pleaded guilty at a summary court-martial to absence without leave and missing movement. She received thirty days of confinement and demotion to private, while remaining eligible to complete her service. Her case concerns resistance in the context of reported military sexual abuse, rather than a documented conscientious-objector discharge.
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist profiles page identifies Suzanne Swift; available directory portrait is only 100x100. Larger Spokesman/CTR image lead remains open.

profiles.name: Phan Nguyen
profiles.description: Phan Nguyen is a Vietnamese American anti-war organizer and writer who worked with Port Militarization Resistance in Olympia and Tacoma, Washington. Tacoma police arrested him on March 11, 2007 after he tried to enter the designated protest area at the Port of Tacoma carrying a backpack. Prosecutors charged him with disobeying a traffic officer under a rule barring backpacks from the protest zone. The municipal court dismissed the case, and the dismissal was upheld in September 2008. Nguyen later joined a civil-rights suit challenging the arrest and police restrictions. The accessible court record does not state how long he was held.
profiles.finding: PM Press, Truthout and Mondoweiss case/author leads; no verified individual portrait retrieved.

profiles.name: Khalid Awan
profiles.description: Khalid Awan, 50, Pakistani foreign national, was indicted October 25, 2006 for providing material support to KCF (Sikh militants seeking a separate Sikh state). At trial, prison phone calls captured him recruiting for KCF and admitting sending hundreds of thousands of dollars to Paramjit Sing Panjwar in Pakistan. 168 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release.
profiles.finding: Global News 2020 case reporting explicitly captions subject-supplied photograph. Downloaded and visually verified recognizable portrait. TCS Express founder Flickr result rejected as unrelated namesake.

profiles.description: Haji Subandi, 69, Tamil Tigers ICE-sting defendant; emailed an FBI undercover business inquiring about weapons and sent a list of 53 military weapons. 37 months federal prison.
profiles.finding: Liputan6 reporting on Indonesian defendants is a lead; no individual photograph verified. DOJ plea document corroborates case.

profiles.name: Haniffa Bin Osman
profiles.description: Haniffa Bin Osman was a Singaporean arms broker who acted as a middleman between weapons suppliers and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam. He flew to Baltimore in July 2006 to test-fire machine guns, and on September 26, 2006 travelled to Guam to inspect machine guns, sniper rifles, ammunition and two surface-to-air missiles intended for the Tamil Tigers, discussing the commission he stood to earn on the sale; he wired a $752,000 down payment for the weapons. The buyers were undercover federal agents. He pleaded guilty on April 5, 2007 to conspiracy to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization and to money laundering, and was sentenced to 37 months in federal prison followed by three years of supervised release. He was not a member of the LTTE and held no military rank: the retired Indonesian Marine Corps general in the same case was his co-defendant Erick Wotulo, who was sentenced to 30 months and deportation.
profiles.finding: DOJ Singapore broker sentencing page corroborates case; no verified portrait found.

profiles.name: Naudimar Herrera
profiles.description:
Naudimar Herrera was the only Liberty City defendant to be acquitted at the third trial. He was held in federal pretrial detention from his June 23, 2006 arrest through the end of the third trial in May 2009 — nearly three full years in custody — before a federal jury cleared him on all four counts. His acquittal was the only complete acquittal of any Seas of David defendant in the case.

On June 23, 2006, the Federal Bureau of Investigation arrested seven men in the predominantly Haitian-American Liberty City neighborhood of Miami, Florida. They were members of a small religious collective called the Seas of David — founded by Narseal Batiste, the group blended elements of Christianity, the Moorish Science Temple, and Black Hebrew Israelite practice, and met in a warehouse in Liberty City where its members worked construction jobs and studied scripture. Federal prosecutors charged all seven with conspiring with al-Qaeda to blow up the 110-story Sears Tower in Chicago, the FBI's Miami office, and other federal buildings.

The plot was, from the federal government's first contact with the group, manufactured by FBI confidential informants. After receiving an October 2005 tip, the Miami FBI inserted a paid informant (Abbas al-Saidi) into the group's circle, and later a second informant (Elie Assad) posing as an al-Qaeda recruiter. The informants supplied the group with cash, with combat boots, and with the suggestion that they "swear bayat" (an oath of loyalty to Osama bin Laden) — a ceremony staged at the informants' insistence. The defendants never had any actual contact with al-Qaeda, never possessed any weapons or explosives, never traveled to any of the buildings prosecutors said they planned to attack, and never made any concrete steps toward an actual operation. Their case became, alongside the Newburgh Four, one of the two most cited examples of post-9/11 FBI manufactured-plot terrorism prosecutions.

The case went through three federal trials before Judge Joan A. Lenard at the U.S. District Court in Miami. The first trial (October–December 2007) ended in a hung jury and acquittal for Lyglenson Lemorin. The second trial (January–April 2008) also ended in a hung jury for the remaining six defendants. The third trial (January–May 2009) finally produced convictions of Narseal Batiste, Patrick Abraham, Stanley Grant Phanor, Burson Augustin, and Rothschild Augustine, and an acquittal for Naudimar Herrera. The five convicted defendants were sentenced together on November 20, 2009. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the convictions in 2013 over a vigorous dissent that compared the case to the wave of "outrageous government conduct" cases that had once been recognized in U.S. law.

profiles.name: Patrick Abraham
profiles.description:

He was convicted in the third Liberty City trial on multiple counts of conspiracy and sentenced on November 20, 2009 to 112.5 months (9 years and 4 months) in federal prison, followed by 15 years of supervised release. After completion of his federal sentence he was subject to immigration removal to Haiti.

profiles.description:
